problem: Exploration and mapping pipelines maintain detailed geometric maps (occupancy grids) that cost memory, compute and sensing, and existing topological/room-graph methods rely on ad-hoc post-processing of low-level maps without exploiting structural priors of buildings.
motivation: Resource-constrained robots (micro-robots, long-duration missions) need compact, semantic environment representations. Indoor layouts are predictable (rectangular rooms plus doors), so a network can learn these priors and hallucinate unseen structure to guide exploration more efficiently than frontier methods.
key_idea: Use a DETR-style CNN-transformer to predict rooms and doors directly as boxes forming a topological graph from laser scans and the previous graph, trained via a parametric ReLU-based TSDF of the boxes so that no manual box labels are needed.
insight: Because boxes map analytically to a TSDF, training only needs ground-truth occupancy/TSDF maps, and a hierarchical door loss (GT TSDF minus room-only TSDF) helps detect small but topologically important doors. Planning on the hallucinated graph gives shorter trajectories than geometric frontier exploration, at O(M^2) memory versus O(N^2), with only small map-accuracy loss (SSIM 0.96, Hamming 2.4-2.5%). However, the RH strategy over the graph gives no gain over greedy, and an occupancy-based RH baseline (111 steps) is about as short as BoxMap (114.9).
method: Backbone: 4-layer CNN (channels 32/64/128/256; downsampling conv + conv, BatchNorm, LeakyReLU) on the concatenation of the local laser occupancy map and the occupancy map instantiated from the previous topological graph.
Transformer: 4 encoder and 4 decoder layers with M randomly initialised box queries producing M embeddings in parallel (DETR-like, no NMS or anchors).

Prediction heads: room heads predict box existence and coordinates; an adjacency matrix from overlapping box edges (N/S/W/E) is computed; door heads operate on outer sums of embedding pairs, predicting door existence (masked by adjacency) and door box relative to the shared edge.

Parametric TSDF: L-infinity rectangle TSDF written with ReLU functions, boxes merged by max (multi-box for non-rectangular rooms, door as square box on shared edges), making box-to-TSDF differentiable.

Losses: TSDF L2 loss, wall-masked boundary loss, hierarchical door loss (GT TSDF minus room-only TSDF, diamond door TSDF), self-supervised IoU loss between room boxes, and a gate loss (bimodal + sparsity) on box existence.

Graph-based exploration: build a planning graph (door nodes, room nodes placed between centroid and door) and pick the next unvisited room via Greedy (closest) or Receding Horizon (DP shortest tour of all unvisited rooms), then A* on an accumulated occupancy map; update the graph after reaching each goal.
Training data: RPLAN floorplans with TSDF from chamfer distance transform; the model is trained on occupancy maps and then fine-tuned on predicted-environment inputs.

setting.training_data: 400 RPLAN floorplans (5 rooms each), 128x128 local maps from frontier-exploration trajectories, 41 for test; first trained on occupancy maps, then fine-tuned on predicted-graph inputs
setting.observation: 2-D laser scan (360° FoV, 9 m range) converted to a local occupancy map, plus previous topological graph
setting.action_space: graph-level goals (next unvisited room), executed by A* on an occupancy grid
setting.simulator: PseudoSLAM (HouseExpo) for main experiments; Gazebo/ROS with Jackal for a qualitative demo
setting.privileged: none at test time (assumes map alignment/dominant wall direction detected and fairly accurate odometry)

numbers.eval_set_note: 41 test environments x 3 random initial positions
41 test environments x 3 random initial positions

numbers_note: Custom benchmark (RPLAN, 5-room houses) with no standard embodied-navigation benchmark. The abstract's 30.9% shorter trajectories is versus the standard frontier baseline (166.4 steps in Table 1); it is not a per-row number.
results: On 41 test environments x 3 starts, BoxMap needs 114.9 (Greedy) / 115.2 (RH) steps versus 166.4 for standard frontier exploration (C3, about 30.9% shorter) and 143.6 for the map-completion baseline (C4), with O(M^2) memory instead of O(N^2). The strongest baseline, occupancy-map RH (C5), is slightly shorter at 111 steps but uses the full geometric map. Reconstructed map quality stays high (SSIM 0.96, Hamming 2.4-2.5%).
limitations: Evaluated only on small synthetic 5-room RPLAN floorplans in 2-D, assuming known map alignment and accurate odometry; no real-robot tests (only a qualitative Gazebo demo).
The model can forget visited entities over long horizons because low-level geometry is discarded; errors are corrected only by revisiting, at the cost of longer paths.
Occupancy-based RH baseline (111 steps) matches or slightly beats BoxMap in path length; small doors remain hard to detect.
builds_on: Wang et al. 2023 multi-task multi-level abstraction (map completion)
compares_to: Frontier exploration with learned map completion (Shrestha et al. 2019)
